name: Kestrel Fold

detectability.signature: A needle-thin line of compressed starfield flanked by subspace shear harmonics

proximity: The starfield visibly compresses ahead of the corridor like light bending down a drain
Navigation instruments begin offering contradictory position solutions
contact: Entering vessels report a brief sensation of falling sideways
Hull-mounted sensors lose fix on normal space for two to five seconds
prolonged_exposure: Ships lingering in the corridor drift toward whichever exit point is currently dominant
Extended transit leaves compass gyros precessing for hours afterward

phenomena: Ships exit at locations up to hundreds of kilometers from the plotted exit point
The starfield within the corridor distorts into parallel streaks
Navigation consoles display two simultaneous, equally confident position fixes
hazards: Exit-point scatter depositing vessels well off their plotted course
Disorientation from sustained contradictory instrument readings
opportunities: Shortcut through normal space shaving eleven days off the Meridian Run
Emergency escape route usable when conventional lanes are blocked
Access to otherwise unreachable regions beyond the Corvane Shelf
known_incidents: A courier run in 2411 exited forty thousand kilometers off its plotted exit, prompting construction of the present beacon network
description: The Kestrel Fold presents itself as a needle of pinched starlight forty kilometers across, a place where distant galaxies appear stacked like pages pressed together. Its mouth shimmers faintly violet, and subspace sensors hear a thin shear harmonic running the length of the corridor. It looks less like a hole in space than a seam someone forgot to finish sewing.

Transit is fast and generally uneventful: a few seconds of sideways falling, a stretch of streaked stars, and arrival eleven days closer to one's destination than any conventional route allows. The fold's temper shows only at the exit, where it deposits ships anywhere within a few hundred kilometers of the nominal point, and it wanders its own length by a kilometer or two each month. Beacon buoys bracketing both mouths re-survey the alignment weekly.

Xenoarchaeologists attribute the fold to a precursor relay that failed catastrophically some three centuries ago, folding two distant points together instead of bridging them cleanly. The 2411 courier incident, in which a mail packet exited forty thousand kilometers off station, led directly to the beacon network that makes the passage commercially reliable. Despite its quirks, the fold has carried over ninety thousand transits without a single lost vessel.

Guild pilots treat the Kestrel Fold with the fond exasperation reserved for an old ship that mostly behaves. Survey teams periodically probe the corridor's walls, hoping to learn whether the precursor mechanism can be stabilized or replicated. For merchants on the Meridian Run, the arithmetic is simple: eleven days saved, a modest scatter risk, and the best view of folded spacetime this side of a physics lecture.
